ADVERTISEMENT.


THE following Abridgment has been made from the larger Lexicon pub-
\whed at the University Press.


It has been reduced to its present compass by the omission—


I. Of passages cited as Authorities, except where examples were necessary
to explain more clearly the usage of a word.


II. Of discussions upon the Derivation of words.


III. Of words used only by late authors, or of the particular meanings of
words not in general use, such as medical or scientific terms: but words
used oy Theocritus, the writers of the Anthology, Lucian, and Plutarch
in his Lives, have been retained; and especial care has been taken to
explain all words contained in the New Testament.


Words are printed in Capitals, when they are radical forms, or when no
form nearer the original Root is known to exist. In other words, the Derivation,
when it can be sufficiently ascertained, is usually placed before the meaning :
when this is not the case, some notice will be found at the end of the word.


Many additional tenses and cases, mostly Homeric or Doric, have been
inserted to give a clue to the simple word, when there seemed to be any diffi-
ealty or irregularity in the formation. The quantity of doubtful syllables has
been marked, except in the case of tenses of Verbs, cases of Nouns, and words
derived according to grammatical rule.


The present Edition has been revised throughout, from the fourth Edition of
the original Work.

For the sake of clearness, the parts of which compound words are made up
have been marked by placing a hyphen between them, as, dzo-BddAw, &g-(yu,
&-Saros, €f-od0s. But when a word is compounded of two parts, one of which is
already a compound, this latter compound 1s left undivided, and must be sought
m its own place, as pi\0-xiccopdpos. And a word immediately derived from a
compound is left undivided, so that the composition must be sought under the
word from which it is derived, as giAopoveéw, dtAd-povocos. In Verbs com-
pounded of a Preposition and a simple Verb, mere division has been considered
sufficient to mark the formation, as also in some Nouns formed from a Prepo-
sition and a simple Noun. |


All tenses and forms of words in the Gospels that presented any difficulty have
been inserted in their place.

The ancient Choral Dance of Greece, which


originated among tho Dorians, reached its perfection
in the yopds xuxd:xus performed at the Athenian
Dionysia. This Chorus consisted of 50 persons.
Hence arose the Attic Drama, which consisted at
first of mere tales in the intervals of the Dance,
told by asingle Actur. The Chorus was then distin-
guished into three principal kinds, the xdpos rpayi-
«és consisting of 12 or 15 persons, the xopurds of 24,
and the carupxdés. When a Poet wished to bring
out a piece, the Archon granted him a Chorus (xo-
pov axe) the expenses of which were defrayed by
some rich citizen, hence called yopryés : the Chorus
was regularly trained by the Poet himself, who was
hence called yopodddoxados.

The ancient Choral Dance of Greece, which
originated among the Dorians, reached its perfection
in the xopds xuxducus performed at the Athenian
Dionysia. This Chorus consisted of 50 persons.
Hence arose the Attic Drama, which consisted at
first of mere tales in the intervals of the Dance,
told by asingle Actur. The Chorus was then distin-
guished into three principal kinds, the ydpos rpayt-
ads consisting of 12 or 15 persons, the rapuxds of 24,
and the carupx«és. When a Poet wished to bring
out a piece, the Archon granted him a, Chorus (xo-
pov éaxe) the expenses of which were defrayed by
some rich citizen, hence called xopiyds : the Chorus
was regularly trained by the Poet himself, who was
hence called yopod:ddanados.
